steps.text: Define L=[[I,0],[CA⁻¹,I]], H=[[A,0],[0,S]], and U=[[I,A⁻¹B],[0,I]]. Direct block multiplication gives LH=[[A,0],[C,S]]. Therefore LHU=[[A,B],[C,CA⁻¹B+S]]=M.

If S is invertible, then H⁻¹=[[A⁻¹,0],[0,S⁻¹]]. Both HH⁻¹ and H⁻¹H equal the identity. Thus U⁻¹H⁻¹L⁻¹ is a two-sided inverse of LHU=M.
If M is invertible, then H=L⁻¹MU⁻¹ is invertible, with inverse UM⁻¹L. Write its inverse as [[E,F],[G,J]]. The bottom-right blocks of HH⁻¹=I and H⁻¹H=I give SJ=JS=I. Thus S is invertible.
Multiply U⁻¹H⁻¹ to obtain [[A⁻¹,−A⁻¹BS⁻¹],[0,S⁻¹]]. Its product with L⁻¹ is the displayed inverse. The order of every factor matters. No interchange of matrix factors occurs.

The first block equation is Ax+By=f. Since A is invertible, x=A⁻¹(f−By). Substitute this into Cx+Dy=g to obtain Sy=g−CA⁻¹f. Conversely these two reduced equations imply both original equations. Empty blocks satisfy the same identities.

steps.text: For bounded operators U and V, ‖UVx‖≤‖U‖‖V‖‖x‖. Thus ‖UV‖≤‖U‖‖V‖. Induction gives ‖Tⁿ‖≤qⁿ for n≥1. Also ‖I‖≤1, including the zero space.

Let P_N=∑_{n=0}^N Tⁿ. For m>N, the triangle inequality gives ‖P_m−P_N‖≤∑_{n=N+1}^m qⁿ≤q^(N+1)/(1−q). The linked scalar geometric series proves that this bound tends to 0. Hence the partial sums form a Cauchy sequence in operator norm.

For each x, the sequence P_Nx is Cauchy because ‖(P_m−P_N)x‖≤‖P_m−P_N‖‖x‖. Completeness of E gives a limit Rx. Limits preserve addition and scalar multiplication, so R is linear. The bound ‖P_Nx‖≤(∑_{n=0}^N qⁿ)‖x‖ gives ‖Rx‖≤‖x‖/(1−q). Thus R is bounded.

For every x, take m→∞ in the tail estimate to obtain ‖(R−P_N)x‖≤q^(N+1)‖x‖/(1−q). Continuity of the norm follows from |‖u‖−‖v‖|≤‖u−v‖. The definition of operator norm gives the stated tail bound and proves P_N→R in operator norm.

Finite cancellation gives (I−T)P_N=P_N(I−T)=I−T^(N+1). The operator norm of T^(N+1) is at most q^(N+1), which tends to 0. Products with the fixed bounded operator I−T preserve operator-norm limits by the first-step bound. Therefore (I−T)R=R(I−T)=I.
The tail and inverse bounds also hold when q=0. In that case T=0, R=I, and every tail is 0. The proof does not require different operators to commute. It uses only powers of T.

worked_application.goal: Solve u(x)−(1/2)∫₀ˣu(t)dt=1 for x in [0,1], and bound a finite approximation.
hypotheses: E=C([0,1],ℝ) with the uniform norm is complete.
Define (Tu)(x)=(1/2)∫₀ˣu(t)dt. This operator is linear and maps continuous functions to continuous functions.

Completeness follows directly: a uniform Cauchy sequence has pointwise real limits. The same Cauchy estimate proves uniform convergence. For a point x, select one continuous approximant within ε/3 of the limit. Its continuity and the triangle inequality prove continuity of the limit at x.

steps.text: For ‖u‖∞≤1, |(Tu)(x)|≤x/2≤1/2. The function u=1 attains 1/2 at x=1. Thus ‖T‖=1/2.

  simp only [gaussSum, AddChar.inv_apply, Finset.sum_mul, Finset.mul_sum, MulChar.inv_apply']
  conv =>

steps.text: Every nonzero character value has finite multiplicative order because its source group is finite. Thus |χ(x)|=1 for x≠0 and |ψ(x)|=1 for all x. Their complex conjugates equal their inverses.
Choose a∈F× with χ(a)≠1. The bijection x↦ax on F× shows ∑_{x∈F×}χ(x)=χ(a)∑_{x∈F×}χ(x). Subtract the two sides and divide by 1−χ(a). Therefore the multiplicative character sum is 0.

Choose z∈F with ψ(z)≠1. The bijection x↦x+z gives ∑_{x∈F}ψ(x)=ψ(z)∑_{x∈F}ψ(x), so this additive character sum is 0. If b≠0, multiplication by b permutes F. Hence ∑_{y∈F}ψ(by)=0. Remove the y=0 term to obtain ∑_{y∈F×}ψ(by)=−1. For b=0 the latter sum is q−1.

Expand |G|²=G conjugate(G) as a finite double sum. Terms with x=0 or y=0 vanish. For each y≠0, write x=ty. This bijection changes χ(x)conjugate(χ(y)) to χ(t), and ψ(x)conjugate(ψ(y)) to ψ((t−1)y). Thus |G|²=∑_{t∈F×}χ(t)∑_{y∈F×}ψ((t−1)y).
Separate t=1. Its inner sum is q−1 and χ(1)=1. Every other t contributes −χ(t). The zero sum in step 2 gives ∑_{t≠0,1}χ(t)=−1. Therefore |G|²=(q−1)−(−1)=q.

If χ²=1 on F×, all its values are real and equal to 1 or −1. Therefore conjugate(G)=∑χ(x)ψ(−x). Replace x by −x to obtain conjugate(G)=χ(−1)G. Since χ(−1)²=1, the magnitude equation yields χ(−1)G²=q, or G²=χ(−1)q.

worked_application.goal: Compute ∑_{x=0}^4 exp(2πiax²/5) for a=1 and a=2.
hypotheses: F=ℤ/5ℤ is a field. Put ζ=exp(2πi/5) and ψ(t)=ζᵗ.

The squares x² for x=0,1,2,3,4 are 0,1,4,4,1. Thus the number of roots of x²=t is 1+χ(t) for each t in F. For a≠0, the additive-character sum ∑_tψ(at) is 0. Therefore S(a)=∑_tχ(t)ψ(at).

lemma LocalizedModule.map_exact (g : M₀ →ₗ[R] M₁) (h : M₁ →ₗ[R] M₂) (ex : Exact g h) :
    Exact (map S (mkLinearMap S M₀) (mkLinearMap S M₁) g)
    (map S (mkLinearMap S M₁) (mkLinearMap S M₂) h) :=
  fun y ↦ Iff.intro
    (induction_on
      (fun m s hy ↦ by
        rw [map_LocalizedModules, ← zero_mk 1, mk_eq, one_smul, smul_zero] at hy
        obtain ⟨a, aS, ha⟩ := Subtype.exists.1 hy
        rw [smul_zero, mk_smul, ← map_smul, ex (a • m)] at ha
        rcases ha with ⟨x, hx⟩
        use mk x (⟨a, aS⟩ * s)
        rw [map_LocalizedModules, hx, ← mk_cancel_common_left ⟨a, aS⟩ s m, mk_smul])
      y)
    fun ⟨x, hx⟩ ↦ by
      revert hx
      refine induction_on (fun m s hx ↦ ?_) x
      rw [← hx, map_LocalizedModules, map_LocalizedModules, (ex (g m)).2 ⟨m, rfl⟩, zero_mk]

steps.text: The induced map is well-defined. If u(tm−sn)=0, linearity gives u(tf(m)−sf(n))=0. The same u proves equality of the image fractions. Composition commutes with localization by evaluation on every fraction.
Since gf=0, the image of S⁻¹f lies in the kernel of S⁻¹g. Conversely let n/s satisfy g(n)/s=0. The definition of equality of fractions gives u∈S with ug(n)=0. Thus g(un)=0.

worked_application.goal: Localize 0→ℤ→ℤ→ℤ/6ℤ→0, whose first nonzero map is multiplication by 6, at powers of 2.
hypotheses: R=ℤ and S={2ⁿ:n≥0}. Multiplication by 6 is injective, and its image is the kernel of reduction modulo 6.

The class of 3 in ℤ/6ℤ disappears because 2·3=0. The class of 2 remains nonzero and has order 3. If all nonzero integers are inverted instead, multiplication by 6 is invertible and the quotient becomes 0.

steps.text: The determinant for n=0 is 1, which agrees with the empty product. For n=1 it is also 1. Assume the formula for n−1 and first take distinct nodes a₀,…,aₙ₋₂.

Replace the last node by an indeterminate X. Expand the determinant along its last row. This gives a polynomial D(X) of degree at most n−1. Its leading coefficient is the determinant of the first n−1 nodes, because the last cofactor has positive sign.
For X=aᵢ with i<n−1, two rows are equal and D(aᵢ)=0. This equality follows from the determinant definition: interchange those rows in each permutation term and pair terms with opposite signs.

For any polynomial P, the identity Xᵏ−aᵏ=(X−a)∑_{j=0}^{k−1}Xᵏ⁻¹⁻ʲaʲ shows P(X)−P(a) is divisible by X−a. Therefore each distinct root aᵢ gives a factor X−aᵢ. After division by earlier factors, evaluation at a later root still gives 0, since the earlier factors are nonzero there.

Thus D(X) is its leading coefficient times ∏_{i<n−1}(X−aᵢ). The induction hypothesis supplies that coefficient. Substitute X=aₙ₋₁ to obtain the full product. If the first n−1 nodes are not distinct, V has repeated rows, and both sides are 0.

If det(V)≠0, its adjugate gives the inverse V⁻¹=adj(V)/det(V). The adjugate identity follows by cofactor expansion: diagonal entries give det(V), and off-diagonal entries give determinants with a repeated row. If det(V)=0, the nodes repeat and V has two equal rows, so V cannot map onto every data vector. The interpolation equations are Vc=y. Thus distinct nodes give exactly one coefficient vector c.

steps.text: The matrix A*A is Hermitian because (A*A)*=A*A. It is positive semidefinite because v*A*Av=‖Av‖²≥0. The linked spectral theorem gives an orthonormal basis vᵢ of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues λᵢ≥0.
Order the positive eigenvalues first, and set σᵢ=√λᵢ. For λᵢ>0 define uᵢ=Avᵢ/σᵢ. Then ⟨uᵢ,uⱼ⟩=⟨vᵢ,A*Avⱼ⟩/(σᵢσⱼ)=λⱼδᵢⱼ/(σᵢσⱼ)=δᵢⱼ. Thus these uᵢ are orthonormal.

If λᵢ=0, then ‖Avᵢ‖²=λᵢ‖vᵢ‖²=0, so Avᵢ=0. Expansion in the vᵢ basis shows that the range of A is exactly the span of the positive-eigenvalue uᵢ. Its dimension is the number of those eigenvalues, namely r.

Extend the r orthonormal vectors uᵢ to an orthonormal basis of ℂᵐ. If their span is proper, choose a vector outside it. Subtract its orthogonal projections onto the existing vectors. The remainder is nonzero and orthogonal to them. Normalize it, and repeat until m vectors exist.
Let U and V have these basis vectors as columns. They are unitary. The equations Avᵢ=σᵢuᵢ for i≤r and Avᵢ=0 otherwise show U*AV=Σ. Multiply by U and V* to obtain A=UΣV*.
For x=∑cᵢvᵢ, orthonormality gives ‖Ax‖²=∑_{i≤r}σᵢ²|cᵢ|²≤σ₁²‖x‖². Equality holds for x=v₁ if r>0. If r=0, A=0. This proves the operator norm formula.

steps.text: Compute A*A=[[1,1],[1,2]]. Its characteristic polynomial is λ²−3λ+1. The eigenvalues are λ±=(3±√5)/2, both positive.

The two left singular vectors span the first 2 coordinate directions. Add (0,0,1) to obtain U. These vectors and the vλ give A=UΣV*. The largest amplification is φ, and the smallest amplification on the domain is φ⁻¹.

The Euclidean condition number for this full-column-rank map is their ratio φ²=(3+√5)/2. The determinant of its top 2×2 block is 1, but this does not force equal amplification in different directions.

Tonelli gives Γ(a)Γ(b)=∫_{(0,∞)²}u^(a−1)v^(b−1)e^(−u−v)dudv. The integrand is nonnegative, so the factorization is valid.

Use u=rs and v=r(1−s), with r>0 and 0<s<1. The inverse map is r=u+v and s=u/(u+v), so this is a smooth bijection. Its absolute Jacobian is r. The change-of-variables formula gives the integrand r^(a+b−1)e^(−r)s^(a−1)(1−s)^(b−1).
Tonelli factors the transformed integral into Γ(a+b)B(a,b). Divide by the positive Γ(a+b) to obtain the ratio formula.

Put φ(x)=e^(−x²/2). Since φ′=−xφ, induction and the product rule give φ^(n)=(-1)ⁿHₙφ. The induction step is D((-1)ⁿHₙφ)=(-1)ⁿ(Hₙ′−xHₙ)φ=(-1)ⁿ⁺¹Hₙ₊₁φ.

Every polynomial times φ is integrable, and tends to 0 at ±∞. For each integer k≥0, |x|ᵏe^(−x²/2) has a finite integral. For large |x|, k log|x|≤x²/4, so the expression is at most e^(−x²/4). The linked Gaussian integral proves that bound is integrable. This also proves the boundary limit.

On each finite interval, integrate Hₘφ^(n) by parts n times. Then send both endpoints to infinity. Every boundary term is a polynomial times φ, so step 3 makes it vanish. Absolute integrability permits the improper limits. The two factors (-1)ⁿ cancel, giving ∫HₘHₙφ=∫Hₘ^(n)φ.
If n>m, the nth derivative of Hₘ is 0, so the integral is 0. If n=m, monicity gives Hₙ^(n)=n!, and the linked Gaussian integral gives n!√(2π).
If n<m, interchange m and n in the integral and use the n>m case. Multiplication of the real polynomial values is commutative. This covers every pair of indices, including m=n=0.

Suppose that `φ : E → ℝ` has a local extremum on the set `{x | ∀ i, f i x = f i x₀}` at `x₀`.

Then the derivatives `f' i : E → L[ℝ] ℝ` and `φ' : StrongDual ℝ E` are linearly dependent:
there exist `Λ : ι → ℝ` and `Λ₀ : ℝ`, `(Λ, Λ₀) ≠ 0`, such that `∑ i, Λ i • f' i + Λ₀ • φ' = 0`.

See also `IsLocalExtrOn.linear_dependent_of_hasStrictFDerivAt` for a version that
states `¬LinearIndependent ℝ _` instead of existence of `Λ` and `Λ₀`. -/
theorem IsLocalExtrOn.exists_multipliers_of_hasStrictFDerivAt {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    {f : ι → E → ℝ} {f' : ι → StrongDual ℝ E} (hextr : IsLocalExtrOn φ {x | ∀ i, f i x = f i x₀} x₀)

  let := Classical.decEq ι
  replace hextr : IsLocalExtrOn φ {x | (fun i => f i x) = fun i => f i x₀} x₀ := by
    simpa only [funext_iff] using hextr
  rcases hextr.exists_linear_map_of_hasStrictFDerivAt (hasStrictFDerivAt_pi.2 fun i => hf' i)

steps.text: Let G=(f,φ):U→ℝ^(m+1). Write J for the (m+1)×n matrix of DG(x₀). Its rows are ∇f₁(x₀),…,∇fₘ(x₀),∇φ(x₀). A nontrivial vanishing combination of the rows is exactly the claimed relation. So it is enough to show that the rows are linearly dependent.

Suppose, for a contradiction, that the rows of J are linearly independent. Then J has rank m+1, so its kernel K has dimension n−m−1. Choose a linear map L:ℝⁿ→ℝ^(n−m−1) whose restriction to K is an isomorphism (for example, the orthogonal projection onto K followed by a coordinate isomorphism). If Jx=0 and Lx=0, then x∈K and L|_K x=0, so x=0. Thus x↦(Jx,Lx) is an injective linear map ℝⁿ→ℝⁿ, hence bijective.

Define Ĝ:U→ℝⁿ by Ĝ(x)=(G(x),L x). It is C¹, and DĜ(x₀)=(J,L) is invertible by step 2. The inverse function theorem gives open sets V∋x₀ and W∋Ĝ(x₀) such that Ĝ:V→W is a C¹ bijection with continuous inverse.

Put y₀=Ĝ(x₀)=(f(x₀),φ(x₀),Lx₀). For small real t, the point y_t=(f(x₀),φ(x₀)+t,Lx₀) lies in W, because W is open. Let x_t=Ĝ⁻¹(y_t)∈V. The first m coordinates of Ĝ(x_t) show f(x_t)=f(x₀), so x_t∈S. The next coordinate shows φ(x_t)=φ(x₀)+t.

The inverse is continuous, so x_t→x₀ as t→0. Thus there are points of S arbitrarily close to x₀ with φ>φ(x₀) (take t>0) and points with φ<φ(x₀) (take t<0). This contradicts the local extremum hypothesis. So the rows of J are dependent, which proves the first claim.

Now assume ∇f₁(x₀),…,∇fₘ(x₀) are independent. In a nontrivial relation λ₀∇φ+∑λᵢ∇fᵢ=0, the case λ₀=0 would give a nontrivial relation among the ∇fᵢ, which is impossible. So λ₀≠0. Divide by λ₀ to get λ₀=1 and ∇φ(x₀)=−∑μᵢ∇fᵢ(x₀) with μᵢ=λᵢ/λ₀.

worked_application.title: Extreme values of xy+yz on the unit sphere
worked_application.goal: Find the maximum and the minimum of φ(x,y,z)=xy+yz on S={x²+y²+z²=1}, and the points where they occur.
hypotheses: n=3, m=1, f(x,y,z)=x²+y²+z²−1 and φ(x,y,z)=xy+yz. Both are polynomial, so both are C¹.
∇f=(2x,2y,2z) is nonzero at every point of S, so the independence hypothesis holds at each point.
S is closed and bounded, hence compact, so φ attains a maximum and a minimum on S.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: At an extremum point of the compact set S, the rule gives ∇φ=μ∇f with a real μ. This turns an optimization over a surface into algebraic equations in x,y,z,μ.

steps.text: Compute ∇φ=(y, x+z, y). The rule gives y=2μx, x+z=2μy and y=2μz. The point also satisfies x²+y²+z²=1.
Case y=0. The first and third equations give 2μx=0 and 2μz=0. If μ≠0, then x=z=0 and the constraint fails (the point would be 0). So μ=0, and the middle equation gives x+z=0. Then φ=y(x+z)=0.
Case y≠0. The first and third equations give 2μx=y=2μz, so μ≠0 and x=z=y/(2μ). The middle equation becomes y/μ=2μy, so μ²=1/2 and μ=±1/√2.
For μ=1/√2: x=z=y/√2. The constraint gives y²/2+y²+y²/2=2y²=1, so y=±1/√2 and x=z=y/√2=±1/2. At (1/2,1/√2,1/2) we get φ=y(x+z)=(1/√2)(1)=√2/2. The opposite point gives the same value.
For μ=−1/√2: x=z=−y/√2. The constraint again gives y=±1/√2. At (−1/2,1/√2,−1/2) we get φ=(1/√2)(−1)=−√2/2. The opposite point gives the same value.

The critical values are 0, √2/2 and −√2/2. By compactness the largest and smallest critical values are the global extrema. This agrees with the eigenvalues 0, ±1/√2 of the symmetric matrix [[0,1/2,0],[1/2,0,1/2],[0,1/2,0]] of the form xy+yz.

worked_application.result: The maximum of xy+yz on the unit sphere is √2/2, at ±(1/2,1/√2,1/2). The minimum is −√2/2, at ±(−1/2,1/√2,−1/2).

steps.text: Let p be a prime. Suppose p divides every coefficient of fg, with f and g primitive. Reduce modulo p. The ring 𝔽ₚ[x] is an integral domain, and f̄ḡ=0, so f̄=0 or ḡ=0. Then p divides all coefficients of f or of g. This contradicts primitivity. So fg is primitive. This proves (1).

Prove (2), direction "ℤ irreducible ⇒ ℚ irreducible". Let f be primitive and irreducible in ℤ[x]. Then deg f≥1, since a constant primitive polynomial is ±1, a unit. Suppose f=GH in ℚ[x] with deg G≥1 and deg H≥1.
Clear denominators. Write G=(a/b)G₁ and H=(c/d)H₁, where G₁,H₁∈ℤ[x] are primitive and a/b, c/d are nonzero rationals. Then f=(ac/bd)G₁H₁ with G₁H₁ primitive by (1).

The polynomial f is primitive, and G₁H₁ is primitive. The rational r=ac/bd must have f=rG₁H₁ with integer coefficients. Write r=u/v in lowest terms. Then v divides every coefficient of uG₁H₁ and gcd(v,u)=1, so v divides all coefficients of G₁H₁. Hence v=±1. Also u divides all coefficients of f. Hence u=±1. So r=±1 and f=±G₁H₁ in ℤ[x].
Both G₁ and H₁ have degree at least 1, so neither is a unit of ℤ[x]. This contradicts the irreducibility of f in ℤ[x]. So f is irreducible in ℚ[x].

Prove (2), direction "ℚ irreducible ⇒ ℤ irreducible". Let f be primitive and irreducible in ℚ[x]. Then deg f≥1, so f is not a unit of ℤ[x]. Suppose f=gh in ℤ[x]. In ℚ[x] one factor is a unit, say g=c is a nonzero constant. The integer c divides every coefficient of f. Since f is primitive, c=±1, and g is a unit of ℤ[x]. So f is irreducible in ℤ[x].

Prove (3). Let f be monic with f̄ irreducible in 𝔽ₚ[x]. Then f is primitive, because its leading coefficient is 1. By (2) it is enough to show f is irreducible in ℤ[x]. Suppose f=gh in ℤ[x] with g,h non-units. The leading coefficients multiply to 1, so both equal 1 or both equal −1. Replace (g,h) by (−g,−h) if needed, so g and h are monic.

Both g and h have degree at least 1, since a monic non-unit constant does not exist. Reduce modulo p. We get f̄=ḡh̄ with deg ḡ=deg g≥1 and deg h̄=deg h≥1, because the leading coefficient 1 survives. This is a proper factorization of f̄ in 𝔽ₚ[x]. It contradicts the irreducibility of f̄. So f is irreducible in ℤ[x], and by (2) in ℚ[x].

The field 𝔽₂ has two elements. f̄(0)=1 and f̄(1)=1+1+1=1. So f̄ has no root.
A cubic with a proper factorization has a factor of degree 1, so it has a root. Thus f̄ is irreducible in 𝔽₂[x].
Statement (3) with p=2 shows that f is irreducible in ℚ[x]. So ℚ(α) has degree 3 over ℚ for each root α.
Reduce h modulo 2. We get h̄=x⁴+x+1, because 6≡0 and 3≡1. Then h̄(0)=1 and h̄(1)=1+1+1=1, so h̄ has no root.

steps.text: Orbit-stabilizer count. Fix x in X and let P_x be its stabilizer. The map gP_x ↦ g·x is a well defined bijection from the left cosets of P_x onto the orbit of x. It is well defined and injective because g·x = h·x if and only if h⁻¹g fixes x. So |orbit of x|·|P_x| = |P|.
Orbit sizes. By step 1 the size of each orbit divides |P| = p^n. So each orbit size is a power of p. An orbit has size 1 if and only if its point is fixed. Every other orbit has size divisible by p.
Partition X into orbits. The orbits of size 1 are the points of X^P. The other orbits have sizes divisible by p. Add the sizes: |X| = |X^P| + (a sum of multiples of p). Hence |X| ≡ |X^P| (mod p).
Center. Let P act on the set X = P by conjugation, g·x = gxg⁻¹. A point x is fixed if and only if gxg⁻¹ = x for all g. That means x lies in Z(P). So X^P = Z(P).
Apply step 3 to this action. We get |P| ≡ |Z(P)| (mod p). Because n≥1, we have p | |P|. So p | |Z(P)|.
The identity element lies in Z(P), so |Z(P)| ≥ 1. A positive multiple of p is at least p. So |Z(P)| ≥ p ≥ 2, and Z(P) is not trivial.

Remark. Grouping the conjugation action by orbits (conjugacy classes) gives the class equation |P| = |Z(P)| + ∑ [P : C(x)] over class representatives x outside the center. Step 2 shows that each term of the sum is divisible by p.

worked_application.title: Cauchy theorem from the fixed point congruence
worked_application.goal: Prove that a finite group G with a prime p dividing |G| has an element of order p. Check the count for S₃ and S₄. Also check the center of the dihedral group of order 8.
hypotheses: G is a finite group and p is a prime that divides |G|.
Let X be the set of p-tuples (g₁,…,g_p) in G^p with g₁g₂⋯g_p = e.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The cyclic group C_p of order p is a p-group. It acts on X by rotating the entries. The theorem then counts the fixed points of this action modulo p.

steps.text: Size of X. Choose g₁,…,g_{p−1} freely. Then g_p = (g₁⋯g_{p−1})⁻¹ is forced. So |X| = |G|^{p−1}.
Rotation keeps X. If g₁⋯g_p = e, then g₂⋯g_p g₁ = g₁⁻¹(g₁⋯g_p)g₁ = e. So the rotation (g₁,…,g_p) ↦ (g₂,…,g_p,g₁) maps X to X. It generates an action of C_p.

A tuple is fixed by the rotation if and only if all its entries are equal. The fixed tuples are (g,…,g) with g^p = e. Let N be the number of g in G with g^p = e. The theorem for C_p gives |G|^{p−1} ≡ N (mod p).

Because p divides |G| and p−1 ≥ 1, the left side is divisible by p. So p divides N. The identity satisfies e^p = e, so N ≥ 1. Because p | N, we get N ≥ p ≥ 2. So some g ≠ e has g^p = e. The order of g divides p and is not 1, so it is p.
Check with G = S₃ and p = 3. Here |X| = 6² = 36. The solutions of g³ = e are the identity and the two 3-cycles, so N = 3. Both 36 and 3 are divisible by 3.
Check with G = S₃ and p = 2. Here |X| = 6. The solutions of g² = e are the identity and the three transpositions, so N = 4. Then 6 ≡ 4 ≡ 0 (mod 2).

Check with G = S₄ and p = 3. Here |X| = 24² = 576. The solutions of g³ = e are the identity and the eight 3-cycles, so N = 9. Both 576 = 3·192 and 9 are divisible by 3. A computer enumeration of all tuples agrees with these counts.

Center of the dihedral group D₄ of order 8, acting on the square. Its conjugacy classes have sizes 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, and 1+1+2+2+2 = 8. The center has order 2, which is a multiple of 2. This agrees with the theorem.
The action of D₄ on the four vertices has no fixed vertex. The theorem predicts 4 ≡ 0 (mod 2), which holds.

worked_application.result: Every prime divisor of |G| is the order of some element of G. For S₃ and S₄ the counts N = 3, 4 and 9 match the congruence |G|^{p−1} ≡ N (mod p). The center of D₄ has order 2.

steps.text: G is a p-group, because |G| = p². By the fixed point congruence its center Z has order divisible by p. So |Z| is p or p², by Lagrange.
If |Z| = p², then Z = G and G is abelian. We now show that |Z| = p is impossible. Suppose |Z| = p.
Then |G/Z| = p²/p = p. A group of prime order is cyclic. Indeed any non identity element has an order that divides p, so it has order p and generates the group. So G/Z is cyclic.
Lemma. If G/Z is cyclic for Z = Z(G), then G is abelian. Let gZ generate G/Z. Every x in G has the form x = gⁱz with z in Z, because xZ = (gZ)ⁱ = gⁱZ.

Take x = gⁱz and y = gʲz′ with z, z′ in Z. Then xy = gⁱ z gʲ z′ = gⁱ⁺ʲ z z′, because z commutes with everything. In the same way yx = gʲ⁺ⁱ z′ z. Since z z′ = z′ z and i+j = j+i, we get xy = yx. So G is abelian.
By the lemma, |Z| = p gives G abelian. Then Z = G, so |Z| = p². This contradicts |Z| = p. So the case |Z| = p does not occur, and Z = G.
Classification. Suppose G has an element a of order p². Then G = ⟨a⟩ has p² elements, so G ≅ ℤ/p². Otherwise each non identity element has order p. Pick a ≠ e and b outside ⟨a⟩.

The map (i,j) ↦ aⁱbʲ from ℤ/p × ℤ/p to G is a homomorphism, because G is abelian. It is injective. If aⁱbʲ = e with j ≢ 0 mod p, then b would be a power of a, because j has an inverse mod p and b = b^{jj′} for some j′ with jj′ ≡ 1 (mod p). This contradicts b ∉ ⟨a⟩. So j ≡ 0 and then aⁱ = e gives i ≡ 0. Both groups have p² elements, so the map is an isomorphism.

/-- Euler's Criterion: a nonzero `a : ZMod p` is a square if and only if `x ^ (p / 2) = 1`. -/
theorem euler_criterion {a : ZMod p} (ha : a ≠ 0) : IsSquare (a : ZMod p) ↔ a ^ (p / 2) = 1 := by
  apply (iff_congr _ (by simp [Units.ext_iff])).mp (euler_criterion_units p (Units.mk0 a ha))
  simp only [Units.ext_iff, sq, Units.val_mk0, Units.val_mul]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨y, hy⟩; exact ⟨y, hy.symm⟩
  · rintro ⟨y, rfl⟩
    have hy : y ≠ 0 := by
      rintro rfl
      simp [mul_zero, ne_eq] at ha
    refine ⟨Units.mk0 y hy, ?_⟩; simp

steps.text: Work in the field F = ℤ/p. Because p is odd, for non zero x we have x ≠ −x. Also x² = y² implies (x−y)(x+y) = 0, so y = x or y = −x, because F has no zero divisors.
So the squaring map on F^× is exactly 2 to 1. The set S of non zero squares has (p−1)/2 elements.
Each s in S has the form s = x². Then s^{(p−1)/2} = x^{p−1} = 1 by Fermat little theorem.

So all (p−1)/2 elements of S are roots of the polynomial f = X^{(p−1)/2} − 1. This polynomial has degree (p−1)/2. By the root bound it has at most (p−1)/2 roots. So the roots of f are exactly the elements of S.
Therefore a non zero a is a square if and only if a^{(p−1)/2} = 1. This is the criterion.
For any non zero a put b = a^{(p−1)/2}. Then b² = a^{p−1} = 1 by Fermat. So (b−1)(b+1) = 0 in the field F, and b = 1 or b = −1. For a non square, b ≠ 1, so b = −1.
Square roots for p ≡ 3 (mod 4). Then (p+1)/4 is an integer. If a is a square, a^{(p−1)/2} = 1. Put r = a^{(p+1)/4}. Then r² = a^{(p+1)/2} = a·a^{(p−1)/2} = a.
Remark. For a = −1 we have (−1)^{(p−1)/2} = 1 if and only if (p−1)/2 is even. So −1 is a square modulo p if and only if p ≡ 1 (mod 4).

steps.text: Roots of Xⁿ−1. The n numbers e^{2πik/n}, for k = 0,…,n−1, are distinct and each is a root of Xⁿ−1. A polynomial of degree n has at most n roots. So Xⁿ−1 = ∏_{k=0}^{n−1}(X − e^{2πik/n}), because it is monic.

Order of a root. Let ζ be a root of Xⁿ−1. Its multiplicative order d divides n, because the set of m with ζ^m = 1 is a subgroup of ℤ containing n. Then ζ is a primitive d-th root of unity. Each root has exactly one order.

Group the n linear factors by the order d of the root. For fixed d | n, the roots of order d are exactly the primitive d-th roots of unity. Every primitive d-th root with d | n is a root of Xⁿ−1. So Xⁿ − 1 = ∏_{d|n} ∏_{ζ of order d}(X − ζ) = ∏_{d|n} Φ_d. This proves (1).
Degree. The primitive n-th roots are e^{2πik/n}, where k is in {1,…,n} and gcd(k,n) = 1. Indeed e^{2πik/n} has order n/gcd(k,n). So there are φ(n) of them, and Φ_n has degree φ(n). This proves (2).
Counting degrees in (1): n = ∑_{d|n} φ(d). This proves (4).

Integer coefficients by strong induction on n. Φ_1 = X − 1. Assume that Φ_d is monic with integer coefficients for all d<n. Let g = ∏_{d|n, d<n} Φ_d. This product is monic with integer coefficients, and Xⁿ−1 = g·Φ_n by (1).

Divide Xⁿ−1 by the monic g with remainder in ℤ[X]. We get Xⁿ − 1 = g·q + r with q, r in ℤ[X] and deg r < deg g. Division with remainder by a monic polynomial stays inside ℤ[X]. Also Xⁿ−1 = g·Φ_n, so g(Φ_n − q) = r in ℂ[X]. If Φ_n ≠ q, the left side has degree at least deg g, but deg r < deg g. So r = 0 and Φ_n = q lies in ℤ[X] and is monic. This proves (3).

results.statement: Let M be a monoid and L a field. Let χ₁,…,χ_k : M → L be pairwise distinct monoid homomorphisms from M to the multiplicative monoid of L, so χ(1) = 1 and χ(xy) = χ(x)χ(y). /-- Dedekind's linear independence of characters -/
@[stacks 0CKL]
theorem linearIndependent_monoidHom (G : Type*) [MulOneClass G] (L : Type*) [CommRing L]
    [IsDomain L] : LinearIndependent L (M := G → L) (fun f => f : (G →* L) → G → L) := by
  let := Classical.decEq (G →* L)
  let : MulAction L L := DistribMulAction.toMulAction
  -- We prove linear independence by showing that only the trivial linear combination vanishes.
  apply linearIndependent_iff'.2
  intro s
  induction s using Finset.induction_on with
  | empty => simp
  | insert a s has ih =>
  intro g hg
  -- Here
  -- * `a` is a new character we will insert into the `Finset` of characters `s`,
  -- * `ih` is the fact that only the trivial linear combination of characters in `s` is zero
  -- * `hg` is the fact that `g` are the coefficients of a linear combination summing to zero
  -- and it remains to prove that `g` vanishes on `insert a s`.
  -- We now make the key calculation:
  -- For any character `i` in the original `Finset`, we have `g i • i = g i • a` as functions
  -- on the monoid `G`.
  have h1 (i) (his : i ∈ s) : (g i • i : G → L) = g i • a := by
    ext x
    rw [← sub_eq_zero]
    apply ih (fun j => g j * j x - g j * a x) _ i his
    ext y
    -- After that, it's just a chase scene.
    calc
      (∑ i ∈ s, (g i * i x - g i * a x) • i : G → L) y =
          (∑ i ∈ s, g i * i x * i y) - ∑ i ∈ s, g i * a x * i y := by simp [sub_mul]
      _ = (∑ i ∈ insert a s, g i * i x * i y) -
            ∑ i ∈ insert a s, g i * a x * i y := by simp [Finset.sum_insert has]
      _ = (∑ i ∈ insert a s, g i * (i x * i y)) -
            ∑ i ∈ insert a s, a x * (g i * i y) := by
        congrm ∑ i ∈ insert a s, ?_ - ∑ i ∈ insert a s, ?_
        · rw [mul_assoc]
        · rw [mul_assoc, mul_left_comm]
      _ = (∑ i ∈ insert a s, g i • i : G → L) (x * y) -
            a x * (∑ i ∈ insert a s, (g i • (i : G → L))) y := by simp [Finset.mul_sum]
      _ = 0 := by rw [hg]; simp
  -- On the other hand, since `a` is not already in `s`, for any character `i ∈ s`
  -- there is some element of the monoid on which it differs from `a`.
  have h2 (i) (his : i ∈ s) : ∃ y, i y ≠ a y := by
    by_contra! hia
    obtain rfl : i = a := MonoidHom.ext hia
    contradiction
  -- From these two facts we deduce that `g` actually vanishes on `s`,
  have h3 (i) (his : i ∈ s) : g i = 0 := by
    let ⟨y, hy⟩ := h2 i his
    have h : g i • i y = g i • a y := congr($(h1 i his) y)
    rw [← sub_eq_zero, ← smul_sub, smul_eq_zero] at h
    exact h.resolve_right (sub_ne_zero_of_ne hy)
  -- And so, using the fact that the linear combination over `s` and over `insert a s` both
  -- vanish, we deduce that `g a = 0`.
  have h4 : g a = 0 :=
    calc
      g a = g a * 1 := (mul_one _).symm
      _ = (g a • a : G → L) 1 := by rw [← a.map_one]; rfl
      _ = (∑ i ∈ insert a s, g i • i : G → L) 1 := by
        rw [Finset.sum_insert has, Finset.sum_eq_zero, add_zero]
        simp +contextual [h3]
      _ = 0 := by rw [hg]; rfl
  -- Now we're done; the last two facts together imply that `g` vanishes on every element
  -- of `insert a s`.
  exact (Finset.forall_mem_insert ..).2 ⟨h4, h3⟩

steps.text: Suppose the claim fails. Among all non trivial relations c₁χ₁ + … + c_kχ_k = 0 (for any sub family of the given characters) choose one with the smallest number m of non zero coefficients. After renaming, the relation is c₁χ₁ + … + c_mχ_m = 0 with all c_i ≠ 0.
Case m = 1. Then c₁χ₁(x) = 0 for all x. At x = 1 we get c₁·1 = 0, so c₁ = 0, a contradiction. So m ≥ 2.
Because χ₁ ≠ χ₂, there is h in M with χ₁(h) ≠ χ₂(h).

Apply the relation to the element hx, for any x in M. By multiplicativity, ∑_{i=1}^m c_iχ_i(h)χ_i(x) = 0. Multiply the original relation, evaluated at x, by χ₁(h). We get ∑_{i=1}^m c_iχ₁(h)χ_i(x) = 0.
Subtract the two identities. The term i = 1 cancels. We get ∑_{i=2}^m c_i(χ_i(h) − χ₁(h))χ_i(x) = 0 for all x. This is a relation among χ₂,…,χ_m, with fewer than m non zero terms.
The coefficient of χ₂ is c₂(χ₂(h) − χ₁(h)). It is not 0, because c₂ ≠ 0 and χ₂(h) ≠ χ₁(h). So the new relation is non trivial. This contradicts the minimality of m. So no relation exists.
Automorphisms. A field automorphism σ of F restricts to a monoid homomorphism from the multiplicative monoid of F to F. Distinct automorphisms are distinct functions. So they are independent over F.

steps.text: Each of 1ⁿ, 2ⁿ and 3ⁿ satisfies the recurrence, because each root satisfies the characteristic polynomial. So every combination A + B·2ⁿ + C·3ⁿ satisfies it.

The first three values give a linear system for (A, B, C): A+B+C = 2, A+2B+3C = 7, A+4B+9C = 25. Its matrix is a Vandermonde matrix with nodes 1, 2, 3. Its determinant is (2−1)(3−1)(3−2) = 2, which is not zero.
Solve the system. Subtract the first row from the second: B + 2C = 5. Subtract the second from the third: 2B + 6C = 18, so B + 3C = 9. Then C = 4, B = −3 and A = 1. Check: 1 − 3 + 4 = 2.
So a_n = 1 − 3·2ⁿ + 4·3ⁿ. Both sides satisfy the same recurrence and agree for n = 0, 1, 2. So they agree for all n by induction.
Check the first eight values: 2, 7, 25, 85, 277, 877, 2725, 8365. The recurrence gives the same list from the starting values. For example a₃ = 6·25 − 11·7 + 6·2 = 150 − 77 + 12 = 85.
Uniqueness: if A′ + B′2ⁿ + C′3ⁿ is another closed form, then (A−A′)·1ⁿ + (B−B′)·2ⁿ + (C−C′)·3ⁿ = 0 for all n. By the theorem A = A′, B = B′ and C = C′.

/-- A subgroup of a finite group whose index is the smallest prime factor is normal.

Note : if `G` is infinite, then `Nat.card G = 0` and `(Nat.card G).minFac = 2` -/
theorem normal_of_index_eq_minFac_card (hHp : H.index = (Nat.card G).minFac) :
    H.Normal := by
  by_cases hG0 : Nat.card G = 0
  · rw [hG0, minFac_zero] at hHp
    exact normal_of_index_eq_two hHp
  by_cases hG1 : Nat.card G = 1
  · rw [hG1, minFac_one] at hHp
    exact normal_of_index_eq_one hHp
  suffices H.normalCore.relIndex H = 1 by
    convert H.normalCore_normal
    exact le_antisymm (relIndex_eq_one.mp this) (normalCore_le H)
  have : Finite G := finite_of_card_ne_zero hG0
  have index_ne_zero : H.index ≠ 0 := index_ne_zero_of_finite
  rw [← mul_left_inj' index_ne_zero, one_mul, relIndex_mul_index H.normalCore_le]
  have hp : Nat.Prime H.index := hHp ▸ minFac_prime hG1
  have h : H.normalCore.index ∣ H.index ! := by
    rw [normalCore_eq_ker, index_ker, index_eq_card, ← Nat.card_perm]
    exact card_subgroup_dvd_card (toPermHom G (G ⧸ H)).range
  apply dvd_antisymm _ (index_dvd_of_le H.normalCore_le)
  rwa [← Coprime.dvd_mul_right, mul_factorial_pred hp.ne_zero]
  have hr1 : H.normalCore.index ≠ 1 := fun hr1 ↦ hp.ne_one <|
    Nat.eq_one_of_dvd_one (hr1 ▸ H.normalCore.index_dvd_of_le H.normalCore_le)
  rw [Nat.coprime_factorial_iff hr1]
  exact lt_of_lt_of_le (Nat.sub_one_lt hp.ne_zero) <|
    hHp ▸ minFac_le_of_dvd (Nat.minFac_prime hr1).two_le
      (dvd_trans (minFac_dvd H.normalCore.index) (H.normalCore.index_dvd_card))

steps.text: Let X = G/H be the set of left cosets. It has p elements. The group G acts on X by left multiplication. This action gives a group homomorphism ρ : G → Sym(X) ≅ S_p.
Let K = ker ρ. Then K is a normal subgroup of G. If g is in K, then g fixes the coset H, so gH = H and g is in H. So K ⊆ H.
The first isomorphism theorem gives G/K ≅ ρ(G), a subgroup of S_p. By Lagrange, m = |G/K| divides |S_p| = p!.
Also m = [G:K] divides |G|, because |G| = [G:K]·|K|. So every prime divisor of m divides |G|, hence is at least p by the choice of p.
Every prime divisor of m also divides p! = p·(p−1)!, so it is at most p. Together with step 4, the only prime divisor of m is p. So m = p^a for some a ≥ 0.
The prime p appears in p! exactly once, because the factors 1,…,p each contribute at most one factor p and only p itself does. Since p^a | p!, a ≤ 1. So m is 1 or p.
Now K ⊆ H gives [G:K] = [G:H]·[H:K] = p·[H:K] ≥ p. So m = p and [H:K] = 1. Hence H = K, and H is normal.

Index 2. The same proof with p = 2 uses only that S₂ has order 2. Finiteness of G is used only to say that every prime divisor of m divides |G|. For p = 2 this is not needed, because m divides 2! = 2 already, so the argument works for infinite G.

steps.text: Let K = F^G and n = |G|. Write G = {g₁,…,gₙ}. We show [F:K] ≤ n and [F:K] ≥ n.

Upper bound. Suppose x₁,…,x_m in F are linearly independent over K with m > n. Consider the n equations Σⱼ gᵢ(xⱼ)·yⱼ = 0 for i = 1,…,n, in the m unknowns yⱼ. There are fewer equations than unknowns, so a nonzero solution exists in F.

Choose a nonzero solution with the fewest nonzero entries. Scale it so that one entry equals 1. Apply an element g of G to all equations. Since G permutes the equations, g(y) is again a solution with the same support.
The difference y − g(y) is a solution with fewer nonzero entries, because the entry equal to 1 cancels. By minimality it is zero. So every yⱼ is fixed by G, that is, every yⱼ lies in K.
One equation is the one for the identity element: Σⱼ xⱼ·yⱼ = 0 with yⱼ in K, not all zero. This contradicts the independence of the xⱼ over K. So [F:K] ≤ n.
Lower bound. Suppose [F:K] = m < n, with a K-basis x₁,…,x_m. The m equations Σᵢ gᵢ(xⱼ)·yᵢ = 0 (j = 1,…,m) in n unknowns have a nonzero solution (y₁,…,yₙ) in F.
Every element a of F has the form Σⱼ cⱼxⱼ with cⱼ in K. Each cⱼ is fixed by every gᵢ. So Σᵢ yᵢ·gᵢ(a) = Σⱼ cⱼ·Σᵢ yᵢ·gᵢ(xⱼ) = 0.
So the n distinct automorphisms g₁,…,gₙ satisfy the nontrivial relation Σ yᵢgᵢ = 0 on F. This contradicts the independence of characters. So [F:K] ≥ n, and [F:K] = n.
Consequence. For a subgroup H of G, apply the theorem to H and to G. The degree multiplicativity [F:E][E:K]=[F:K] for a tower K⊆E⊆F gives [F:F^H]·[F^H:F^G] = [F:F^G], so [F^H : F^G] = |G|/|H|.

steps.text: Let n₁,…,n_k generate N over A. Since bN ⊆ N, write b·nᵢ = Σⱼ mᵢⱼ·nⱼ with mᵢⱼ in A. Let M be the matrix (mᵢⱼ).
Let v be the column of the nⱼ. Then (b·I − M)·v = 0 in B^k.
Multiply by the adjugate of (b·I − M). Since adj(X)·X = det(X)·I over a commutative ring, we get det(b·I − M)·nⱼ = 0 for every j.
The element 1 lies in N, so it is a combination of the nⱼ. Hence det(b·I − M)·1 = 0, that is, det(b·I − M) = 0.
Expand the determinant. It is a monic polynomial of degree k in b with coefficients in A. It is the characteristic polynomial of M. So b is integral over A.

Sums and products. Let a and b be integral, with monic equations of degrees r and s. The A-module N spanned by aⁱbʲ with i < r and j < s is finitely generated and contains 1. It is stable under multiplication by a and by b. So a + b and ab satisfy the hypothesis, and they are integral.

steps.text: A nilpotent element lies in every prime ideal. If xⁿ = 0 is in P, then x is in P by repeated use of primality.
Now suppose x is not nilpotent. Let S = {x, x², x³,…}. Then 0 is not in S.
Let Σ be the set of ideals that do not meet S. It is nonempty, because (0) is in it. Order it by inclusion.
A union of a chain of ideals in Σ is an ideal in Σ. By Zorn lemma, Σ has a maximal element P.
We show that P is prime. First, P is proper, because 1 is not in P when x is not in P. Suppose a and b are not in P.
Then P + (a) and P + (b) are bigger than P, so they meet S. We get xᵐ = p + ra and xᵏ = q + sb with p, q in P.
Multiply: xᵐ⁺ᵏ is in P + (ab). If ab were in P, then xᵐ⁺ᵏ would be in P, which contradicts P ∩ S = ∅. So ab is not in P, and P is prime.
Since x is not in P, x is not in the intersection of all primes. So the intersection is contained in the nilradical. For the general form, apply the result to R/I.

steps.text: Counting lemma. Let W=(x0,e1,x1,…,ek,xk) be a trail and w a vertex. The number of edges of W at w equals 2·#{i : 0<i<k, xi=w} plus the number of ends of W that are equal to w. Each inner visit to w uses the two distinct edges ei and ei+1. The start x0 uses only e1, and the end xk uses only ek. No edge is counted twice because W has no repeated edge and G has no loops.

Necessity. Let W be an Euler trail. Then the edges of W at w are all the edges at w, so deg(w) is given by the lemma. If W is closed, both ends equal x0, so deg(x0)=2·(inner visits)+2 is even, and every other degree is even. If W is open from u to v, then deg(u) and deg(v) are odd, and every other degree is even. This proves the "only if" parts of (a) and (b). It also proves the last sentence.

Sufficiency in (a): the trail is closed. Assume all degrees are even. Let W be a trail of maximum length. The number of trails is finite, so W exists. G has an edge, so W has length at least 1. Let W go from a to b. Suppose a≠b. By the lemma the number of edges of W at b is odd, but deg(b) is even. So some edge at b is not in W. Appending it gives a longer trail. This is a contradiction, so a=b and W is closed.

Sufficiency in (a): the trail uses every edge. Suppose some edge e is not in W. All vertices of positive degree lie in one component. So there is a walk from a to an endpoint of e. Append e to this walk. The new walk has at least one edge not in W. Let f be the first such edge. Its first vertex x is a, or the end of an earlier edge that is in W. So x lies on W, and f is an unused edge at x.

Rotate W to start at x. A closed trail through x=xi can be rewritten as xi,…,xk=x0,…,xi. It has the same edges. Appending f gives a closed-then-open trail that is longer than W. This contradicts the maximality of W. So W uses every edge, and W is an Euler circuit.

Sufficiency in (b). Let u≠v be the only vertices of odd degree. Add a new vertex z and the edges zu and zv. In the new graph G′ the degrees of u and v are even, deg(z)=2, and all other degrees are unchanged. So all degrees are even. All vertices of positive degree are still in one component, because z is joined to u. By (a), G′ has an Euler circuit. Rotate it to start at z. Its first and last edges are zu and zv in some order. Reverse the circuit if needed so that it starts with zu. Delete z and these two edges. What remains is a trail from u to v that uses every edge of G exactly once.

results.name: The kernel of the graph Laplacian counts connected components
results.statement: Let G be a finite simple graph on the vertex set V, with adjacency matrix A and degree matrix D. Let L=D−A be the Laplacian. steps.text: Quadratic form. First, xᵀDx=∑_v d(v)x_v². Each edge uv adds x_u² to the term of u and x_v² to the term of v. So xᵀDx=∑_{uv∈E}(x_u²+x_v²). Next, xᵀAx=∑_{(u,v) adjacent} x_u x_v. Each edge appears twice as an ordered pair, so xᵀAx=2∑_{uv∈E} x_u x_v. Subtract: xᵀLx=∑_{uv∈E}(x_u²−2x_ux_v+x_v²)=∑_{uv∈E}(x_u−x_v)².
Positive semidefinite. By step 1, xᵀLx is a sum of squares, so it is not negative. L is symmetric because A and D are symmetric.
If Lx=0, then xᵀLx=0. By step 1 every term (x_u−x_v)² is 0, so x_u=x_v for every edge uv. Along any walk the value of x does not change. So x is constant on each connected component.
Conversely, let x be constant on each component. For a vertex v, (Lx)_v=d(v)x_v−∑_{w∼v}x_w=∑_{w∼v}(x_v−x_w). Each neighbor w of v lies in the component of v, so x_w=x_v. The sum is 0. Hence Lx=0.

By steps 3 and 4, ker L is the set of vectors constant on each component. This space is spanned by the indicators 1_C. They have disjoint supports and are nonzero, so they are linearly independent. Every vector x constant on components equals ∑_C x_C·1_C. Hence dim ker L equals the number c of components, and rank L=|V|−c by rank-nullity.

L is real symmetric, so by the spectral theorem it has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. For a symmetric matrix the multiplicity of the eigenvalue 0 as a root of the characteristic polynomial equals dim ker L. So the eigenvalue 0 has multiplicity c.
The case c=1 gives the last claim: G is connected if and only if dim ker L=1, which holds if and only if rank L=|V|−1.

results.statement: Let G be a finite simple graph with n vertices. Assume G is regular of degree k, any two adjacent vertices have exactly λ common neighbors, and any two distinct non-adjacent vertices have exactly μ common neighbors. steps.text: Walks of length 2. The entry (A²)_{vw} is the number of walks v,x,w of length 2. This is the number of common neighbors of v and w. For v=w it is the degree k. For adjacent v,w it is λ. For distinct non-adjacent v,w it is μ.
The matrix J−I−A has entry 1 exactly at the pairs of distinct non-adjacent vertices, and 0 elsewhere. So the three cases of step 1 say A²=kI+λA+μ(J−I−A). This proves (a).

Apply (a) to the all-ones vector 1. We have A1=k1 and J1=n1. So the left side is A²1=k²1. The right side is (k+λk+μ(n−1−k))1. Hence k²=k+λk+μ(n−k−1). Rearranged, this is k(k−λ−1)=μ(n−k−1). This proves (b).
Rewrite (a) as A²−(λ−μ)A−(k−μ)I=μJ. This follows because μ(J−I−A)=μJ−μI−μA.

Let W be the set of vectors orthogonal to 1. For w∈W, 1ᵀ(Aw)=(A1)ᵀw=k·1ᵀw=0, because A is symmetric. So A maps W to W. On W we have Jw=0. A restricted to W is symmetric, so by the spectral theorem W has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of A.
Let Aw=θw with w∈W and w≠0. Apply the identity of step 4 to w. The left side is (θ²−(λ−μ)θ−(k−μ))w and the right side is μJw=0. So θ²−(λ−μ)θ−(k−μ)=0. This proves (c).

Multiplicities. All eigenvalues of A are k, for the vector 1, together with those on W. Let the two roots of the quadratic be r and s with multiplicities f and g on W. Then f+g=n−1. The trace of A is 0, because G has no loops, so k+fr+gs=0. These two equations determine f and g when r≠s.

/-- An integer Hadamard matrix of order greater than two has order divisible by four.

This is the standard divisibility obstruction in [Section 2.3][deLauneyFlannery2011]. -/
theorem IsHadamard.four_dvd_card {A : Matrix n n ℤ}
    (hA : A.IsHadamard) (hcard : 2 < Fintype.card n) : 4 ∣ Fintype.card n := by
  have hpm : ∀ i j, A i j = 1 ∨ A i j = -1 := fun i j =>
    Unitary.mem_iff_eq_one_or_eq_neg_one.mp (hA.apply_mem i j)
  obtain ⟨r, s, t, hrs, hrt, hst⟩ := Fintype.two_lt_card_iff.mp hcard
  have horth ⦃i k : n⦄ (hik : i ≠ k) : ∑ j, A i j * A k j = 0 := by
    simpa [Matrix.mul_apply, hik] using congr($hA.mul_conjTranspose i k)
  have hexpand : ∀ j, (1 + A s j * A r j) * (1 + A t j * A r j) =
      1 + A s j * A r j + A t j * A r j + A s j * A t j := fun j => by
    obtain hr | hr := hpm r j <;> simp [hr] <;> ring
  have hdvd : ∀ j, (4 : ℤ) ∣ (1 + A s j * A r j) * (1 + A t j * A r j) := fun j => by
    obtain hs | hs := hpm s j <;> obtain hr | hr := hpm r j <;>
      obtain ht | ht := hpm t j <;> simp [hs, hr, ht]
  have hsum : ∑ j, (1 + A s j * A r j) * (1 + A t j * A r j) = (Fintype.card n : ℤ) := by
    simp_rw [hexpand]
    simp [Finset.sum_add_distrib, horth hrs.symm, horth hrt.symm, horth hst]
  rw [← Int.ofNat_dvd, ← hsum]
  exact Finset.dvd_sum fun j _ => hdvd j

steps.text: Normalization. Multiply column j by −1 if the first entry of the first row in column j is −1. This changes no product of two rows, because each column enters the product with a square factor. After this step, the first row has only entries equal to 1.
Row sums. Every other row is orthogonal to the first row. So its entries add up to 0. Hence each other row has the same number of entries 1 and −1. This shows that n is even.

Choose three different rows r1 (the first row), r2 and r3. Such rows exist because n>2. Sort the columns into four classes by the pair (r2 entry, r3 entry). Let a, b, c, d be the sizes of the classes (+,+), (+,−), (−,+), (−,−). Then a+b+c+d=n.
Row r2 has zero sum, so a+b=c+d. Row r3 has zero sum, so a+c=b+d. The rows r2 and r3 are orthogonal, so a+d=b+c. These are the three equations of the proof.
Subtract the second equation from the first. We get b−c=c−b, so b=c. Then the second equation gives a=d. The third equation now reads 2a=2b, so a=b. All four class sizes are equal.
Hence n=a+b+c+d=4a. So n is divisible by 4.

Q is the 11×11 matrix with entry χ(i−j), where χ(x) is 1 for a nonzero square mod 11, −1 for a non-square, and 0 for x=0.

Order 4 and order 8 exist. The Kronecker product of [[1,1],[1,−1]] with itself gives order 4. A third factor gives order 8. A direct check of all 28 pairs of rows of the order-8 matrix gives inner product 0.
Order 12 is divisible by 4, so the theorem does not exclude it. Build the matrix S with S[0][j]=1 and S[j][0]=−1 for j≥1, S[0][0]=0, and S[i+1][j+1]=χ(i−j) for i, j in 0,…,10. Put H=I+S.
Since 11≡3 (mod 4), χ(−1)=−1. Hence Q is skew-symmetric, and S is skew-symmetric. So H has entries 1 and −1 only: the diagonal of S is 0, and every other entry of S is 1 or −1.
Exact integer computation of HHᵀ for all 144 entries gives 12 on the diagonal and 0 off the diagonal. So H is a Hadamard matrix of order 12.
Therefore the orders up to 12 that occur are exactly 1, 2, 4, 8 and 12. Order 12 is the first case where divisibility by 4 holds and a direct power-of-two construction does not give the matrix.

/-- The **Combinatorial Nullstellensatz**.

Given a multi-index `t : σ →₀ ℕ` such that `t s < (S s).card` for all `s`,
`f.totalDegree = t.degree` and `f.coeff t ≠ 0`,
there exists a point `x : σ → R` such that `x s ∈ S s` for all `s` and `f.eval s ≠ 0`.

[Alon_1999], theorem 2 -/
theorem combinatorial_nullstellensatz_exists_eval_nonzero [IsDomain R]
    (f : MvPolynomial σ R)
    (t : σ →₀ ℕ) (ht : f.coeff t ≠ 0) (ht' : f.totalDegree = t.degree)
    (S : σ → Finset R) (htS : ∀ i, t i < #(S i)) :
    ∃ s : σ → R, (∀ i, s i ∈ S i) ∧ eval s f ≠ 0 := by
  let _ : LinearOrder σ := WellOrderingRel.isWellOrder.linearOrder
  by_contra! Heval
  apply ht
  obtain ⟨h, hh, hf⟩ := combinatorial_nullstellensatz_exists_linearCombination S
    (fun i ↦ by rw [← Finset.card_pos]; exact Nat.zero_lt_of_lt (htS i)) f Heval
  rw [hf]
  rw [linearCombination_apply, Finsupp.sum, coeff_sum]
  apply Finset.sum_eq_zero
  intro i _
  set g := h i * Alon.P (S i) i with hg
  by_cases hi : h i = 0
  · simp [hi]
  have : g.totalDegree ≤ f.totalDegree := by
    rw [hg, mul_comm]
    exact hh i
  -- one could simplify this by proving `totalDegree_mul_eq` (at least in a domain)
  rw [hg, ← degree_degLexDegree,
    degree_mul_of_isRegular_right hi (by simp only [(Alon.monic_P ..).leadingCoeff_eq_one,

    Alon.degree_P, map_add, degree_degLexDegree, degree_single, ht'] at this
  rw [smul_eq_mul, coeff_mul, Finset.sum_eq_zero]
  rintro ⟨p, q⟩ hpq
  simp only [Finset.mem_antidiagonal] at hpq
  simp only [mul_eq_zero, Classical.or_iff_not_imp_right]
  rw [← ne_eq, ← mem_support_iff]

  rw [← hpq, map_add, add_lt_add_iff_left, hq, degree_single]
  apply lt_of_le_of_lt _ (htS i)

steps.text: Reduce to |Si|=ti+1. Replace each Si by a subset of size ti+1. A point found in the smaller grid lies in the larger grid. So assume |Si|=ti+1 for all i.
Define gi(xi)=∏_{s∈Si}(xi−s). It is monic of degree ti+1 and it vanishes on Si. Suppose, for contradiction, that f vanishes at every point of the grid.

Division. Divide f by g1 in the variable x1: f=h1g1+f1, where f1 has degree at most t1 in x1. Do the same for x2, …, xn, one after the other. The result is f=Σ hi gi + r, where r has degree at most ti in xi for every i. Each division keeps the total degree at most deg f, and the quotient hi has total degree at most deg f−(ti+1).

The coefficient is unchanged. The part of degree t1+…+tn in the product hi gi is (top part of hi)·xi^{ti+1}. Every monomial in it has xi exponent at least ti+1. The target monomial x^t has xi exponent ti. So it does not occur in hi gi. Hence r has the same coefficient at x^t as f, and this coefficient is not 0.
Vanishing. At each grid point, f is 0 by assumption, and each gi is 0. So r is 0 at each grid point.

Zero lemma. A polynomial r with degree at most ti in xi, and with ti<|Si|, that vanishes on S1×⋯×Sn, is the zero polynomial. Proof by induction on n. Write r=Σ_k ck(x1,…,x_{n−1}) xn^k with k≤tn. For a fixed point of the smaller grid, the one-variable polynomial in xn has degree at most tn and at least tn+1 roots. So it is 0. Hence each ck vanishes on the smaller grid. By induction each ck=0.
By steps 5 and 6, r=0. This contradicts step 4, where the coefficient of x^t in r is nonzero. Hence f does not vanish on the whole grid.

worked_application.title: Cauchy-Davenport over a prime field
worked_application.goal: Show that for sets A, B in Z/p with A+B the set of sums, |A+B| is at least min(p, |A|+|B|−1). Check the claim for three explicit pairs of sets.
hypotheses: p is prime. F=Z/p.
Let a=|A| and b=|B|. Assume a+b−1≤p, since otherwise the bound is p.
Suppose |A+B|≤a+b−2. Take C⊇A+B with |C|=a+b−2. This needs a+b−2≤p.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The polynomial f(x,y)=∏_{c∈C}(x+y−c) vanishes on A×B and has degree a+b−2. Its top monomial coefficient is a binomial. The theorem gives a contradiction when this binomial is nonzero mod p.

steps.text: f has total degree m=a+b−2, because each factor has degree 1. Its top part is (x+y)^m.
Let t1=a−1 and t2=b−1. Then t1+t2=m. The coefficient of x^{a−1}y^{b−1} in (x+y)^m is the binomial coefficient C(m, a−1).
Since m=a+b−2<p, the number C(m, a−1) has no factor p. So it is nonzero in Z/p.
Take S1=A and S2=B. Then |S1|=a>t1 and |S2|=b>t2. The theorem gives (x,y) in A×B with f(x,y)≠0. But x+y∈A+B⊆C, so one factor is 0. This is a contradiction. Hence |A+B|≥a+b−1.
Check 1: p=11, A={0,1,3}, B={0,2,3,7}. Here A+B has 10 elements, and the bound is min(11, 6)=6. The claim holds. The coefficient C(5,2)=10 is nonzero mod 11.

Check 3: p=5, A={0,1,2}, B={0,1,2,3}. Here a+b−1=6>5. The proof does not apply, since C(5,2)=10 is 0 mod 5. The true size is |A+B|=5=p, which agrees with min(p, a+b−1).

steps.text: Converse. A permutation matrix has one entry 1 in each row and column, so it is doubly stochastic. A convex combination of nonnegative matrices with all row and column sums 1 is nonnegative with all row and column sums Σθk=1.
Plan. Induction on the number N of positive entries of M. Each row has a positive entry, so N≥n. We show that M is a convex combination of permutation matrices.

Hall condition on the support. Make a bipartite graph with rows on one side and columns on the other. Join row i to column j if Mij>0. Let R be a set of rows and N(R) the set of columns joined to a row of R. The entries of the rows in R add up to |R|, and all of them lie in columns of N(R). So |R|=Σ_{i∈R,j∈N(R)}Mij≤Σ_{j∈N(R)}Σ_i Mij=|N(R)|. Thus |N(R)|≥|R| for every R. By Hall’s marriage theorem there is a perfect matching: a permutation σ with Mi,σ(i)>0 for all i.
Peeling. Let θ=min_i Mi,σ(i)>0 and let P be the permutation matrix of σ. If θ=1, then each row i has Mi,σ(i)=1. The row sum is 1, so all other entries of row i are 0. So M=P and we are done.

If θ<1, define M′=(M−θP)/(1−θ). The entries of M−θP are not negative, because we subtract θ only at the positions (i,σ(i)) and θ is at most the entry there. Each row sum and column sum of M−θP is 1−θ. So M′ is doubly stochastic.

M′ has fewer positive entries than M. The position (i,σ(i)) where the minimum is attained is positive in M and zero in M′. Entries that are zero in M stay zero in M′. By the induction hypothesis M′ is a convex combination of permutation matrices. Then M=θP+(1−θ)M′ is also one. This proves the first claim.

Extreme points. A permutation matrix P is extreme: if P=tA+(1−t)B with 0<t<1 and A, B doubly stochastic, then at a position where P is 0, both A and B are 0 since entries are nonnegative. At a position where P is 1, both entries are at most 1 and their weighted mean is 1, so both are 1. So A=B=P. Conversely, an extreme point M is a convex combination of permutation matrices, so it equals one of them.

Make the corner nonzero. Choose Mij≠0. If M1j=0, add row i to row 1 (this needs i≠1, and if i=1 then M1j≠0 already). Now M1j≠0. If M11=0 and j≠1, add column j to column 1. Now M11≠0. Call it p.

steps.text: Setup. Let Sk be the k-th partial sum of s for k=0,…,2n+1, with S0=0 and S_{2n+1}=−1. Extend s periodically. Then S_{k+2n+1}=S_k−1 for all k≥0.
The rotation that starts after position m has partial sums S_{m+j}−S_m for j=1,…,2n+1. It has all partial sums negative if and only if S_k<S_m for all k with m<k≤m+2n+1.

Existence. Among 0,…,2n let m be the last index at which S attains its maximum. For m<k≤2n we have S_k<S_m by the choice of m. For 2n+1≤k≤m+2n+1 write k=k′+2n+1 with 0≤k′≤m. Then S_k=S_{k′}−1≤S_m−1<S_m. So the rotation after m has all partial sums negative.

Uniqueness. Suppose that the rotation after m (with 0≤m≤2n) has all partial sums negative. For k′ with 0≤k′≤m, the index k=k′+2n+1 lies in the range (m, m+2n+1], so S_{k′}−1=S_k<S_m. Hence S_{k′}≤S_m. For m<k≤2n we have S_k<S_m by step 2. So m is the last index of the maximum on 0,…,2n, which is a single index.

Counting. A sequence has period dividing 2n+1 only if both counts, n and n+1, are divisible by the number of repeats. Since gcd(n,n+1)=1, a sequence cannot be a repeat of a shorter block, so its 2n+1 rotations are distinct. The set of C(2n+1,n) sequences splits into groups of 2n+1 rotations, and each group has exactly one good member by steps 3 and 4. So the number of good sequences is C(2n+1,n)/(2n+1).
Simplification. C(2n+1,n)/(2n+1)=(2n)!/(n!(n+1)!)=C(2n,n)/(n+1)=Cn.

Dyck words. A good sequence has first step −1 and partial sums S_k<0. Remove the first step. The remaining 2n steps have partial sums S_k+1≤0 and total 0. Negating these steps gives a Dyck word. The map is reversible: a Dyck word, negated and preceded by a step −1, is a good sequence. So the number of Dyck words of semilength n is also Cn.

steps.text: Lifting. The quotient map ℝ→ℝ/ℤ is a covering map with fiber ℤ. By path lifting, each loop γ at x0 has a unique lift γ̃ starting at 0. By homotopy lifting, a homotopy of paths with fixed ends lifts to a homotopy with a fixed starting point.
Integer values. The end point γ̃(1) lies in the fiber over x0, which is ℤ. So w(γ)∈ℤ.

Invariance. Let H be a homotopy of loops at x0 from γ to γ′. Lift H to H̃ with H̃(0,0)=0. The end points H̃(s,1) lie in ℤ and depend continuously on s. A continuous map from [0,1] into the discrete set ℤ is constant. So γ̃(1)=γ̃′(1). Equal winding number follows from homotopy, and w is well defined on π1.
Homomorphism. Let γ and δ be loops with w(γ)=a and w(δ)=b. The lift of the concatenation γ·δ is γ̃ followed by the path δ̃ shifted by a. This path starts at 0 and ends at a+b. So w(γ·δ)=a+b.
Surjective. The loop ωn(t)=nt mod 1 has the lift t↦nt. Its end point is n. So w(ωn)=n.

Injective. Let w(γ)=w(γ′). Their lifts γ̃ and γ̃′ are paths in ℝ from 0 to the same integer. The straight-line homotopy (1−s)γ̃+sγ̃′ fixes both ends. Composing with the quotient map gives a homotopy from γ to γ′ at the base point. Hence w is injective.
So w is a bijective homomorphism, which is the isomorphism π1(S¹,x0)≅ℤ.

worked_application.title: Count the zeros of z⁴+2z+1 with winding numbers
worked_application.goal: Let p(z)=z⁴+2z+1. For a radius r, let wr be the winding number of the loop t↦p(re^{2πit}) around 0. Compute wr for r=0.4, 0.8, 1.2 and 2, and compare with the zeros of p.
hypotheses: The map z↦z/|z| identifies loops in ℂ minus 0 with loops in S¹, up to homotopy.
The winding number around 0 of a loop in ℂ minus 0 is the integer of the theorem for the normalized loop.
p(−1)=1−2+1=0. The other zeros come from the cubic z³−z²+z+1.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The homotopy invariance of the winding number lets us replace p by a simpler polynomial on the circle, as long as no zero of the family lies on the circle.

steps.text: r=2. For s in [0,1] let ps(z)=z⁴+s(2z+1). On |z|=2 we have |z⁴|=16 and |s(2z+1)|≤5. So ps has no zero on the circle. The loops for s=0 and s=1 are homotopic in ℂ minus 0. The loop of z⁴ winds 4 times. So w2=4.
r=0.4. For s in [0,1] let ps(z)=1+s(z⁴+2z). On |z|=0.4 we have |z⁴+2z|≤0.0256+0.8=0.8256<1. So ps has no zero on the circle. The loop for s=0 is constant at 1. So w0.4=0.

r=0.8 and r=1.2. No such simple comparison works, so we sum the changes of argument numerically with 200000 steps. The sums are 1.000000 and 2.000000 in units of 2π, to six places. So w0.8=1 and w1.2=2.

Compare with the zeros. The real zero of the cubic z³−z²+z+1 is about −0.5437. The product of the four zeros is the constant term 1. The two real zeros −1 and −0.5437 have product 0.5437. So the two complex zeros have product 1/0.5437=1.839. They are conjugate, so each has modulus √1.839=1.356.
The zero moduli are 0.5437, 1, 1.356 and 1.356. The counts of zeros inside the circles are 0 for r=0.4, 1 for r=0.8, 2 for r=1.2 and 4 for r=2. These match w0.4, w0.8, w1.2 and w2.
The circle r=1 passes through the zero −1, so the winding number around 0 is not defined there. The jump from 1 to 2 between r=0.8 and r=1.2 comes from that zero.

worked_application.result: The winding numbers are 0, 1, 2 and 4 for r=0.4, 0.8, 1.2 and 2. They equal the number of zeros of p inside each circle.
